opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the right frame is to treat advanced compute somewhat like we treat fissile material. Not identically, since chips are dual-use and have huge economic value, but cutting-edge GPUs are increasingly the key input to capabilities that matter for national security. So the question isn't just market efficiency, it's nonproliferation.

Concretely, I'd separate two goals. First, broad access to AI capabilities, which I think should be widely shared. Countries should be able to use powerful models, build on them, and benefit economically. Second, unrestricted access to the frontier compute needed to train the most dangerous systems, or to run them at scale for things like cyberoffense or bioweapons assistance. That second category deserves much tighter controls.

So in practice that means export controls on the highest-end chips, but also better enforcement, because right now there's a lot of smuggling and diversion. Chips get shipped to shell companies or third countries and end up somewhere else. You'd want things like chip-level location verification, know-your-customer requirements for large clusters, and tracking where large shipments actually go. These are fairly cheap, technically feasible measures that we haven't really implemented seriously.

I'd also add that this isn't purely about keeping chips away from adversaries. There's a stabilizing logic too. If major powers can see roughly how much compute others have and where it is, that transparency reduces the chance that someone makes a bid for a decisive advantage that others feel they have to preempt. So the distribution question connects to deterrence and to avoiding a destabilizing race.

And for allies and most other countries, I'd favor a sort of tiered arrangement: you get access to chips or to cloud compute under verifiable conditions, rather than a blanket yes or no. That keeps the economic benefits flowing while making it much harder for rogue actors, whether states or non-state groups, to accumulate the kind of compute that lets them do catastrophic things.

r001.rationale: The response discusses controlling frontier compute but gives no estimate of 10,000 GPUs as the critical mass for building a state-of-the-art AI system.

r002.rationale: The response favors tiered, verifiable access for allies and other countries, but does not argue that access should favor states based on their responsiveness to deterrence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that compute is really the strategic resource here. If you look at what actually determines who can build frontier AI systems, it's not primarily algorithms, which diffuse pretty quickly, and it's not even data to the same extent. It's whether you can get your hands on tens of thousands of the most advanced chips and the energy to run them. So the question of who gets GPUs is really a question of who gets to be a serious player in AI, and that makes it a geopolitical question, not just an economic one.

My view is that the current regime of export controls makes sense as a starting point. The chips are produced by a very narrow supply chain, essentially TSMC fabricating, ASML providing the lithography tools, Nvidia doing the design. That chokepoint means the US and its allies actually have the ability to shape who gets access, which is unusual. Most dual-use technologies don't have that property. And I think it's reasonable to use that leverage to slow down rivals like China from building the most capable systems, especially given the uncertainty about how those systems would be used.

But I'd push on two things. First, controls on their own aren't sufficient. You need to know where the chips actually end up. Right now there's substantial smuggling and there are intermediaries routing hardware through third countries. So I've argued for things like on-chip mechanisms, essentially hardware-enabled verification, so that a chip can attest to where it is and under what conditions it's being used. That turns export controls from a paper policy into something that's enforceable. Without that you end up with a regime that mostly constrains law-abiding actors and does little to the people you actually care about.

Second, I don't think the goal should be the US racing to build a superintelligence first while denying everyone else. That's the "Manhattan Project" framing, and I think it's dangerous, because if one state gets close to a decisive capability, rivals have strong incentives to sabotage it, and you get escalation. The framing I prefer is something closer to mutual assured AI malfunction, a deterrence dynamic where no state can safely make a unilateral bid for dominance because the others can disrupt it. Compute controls fit into that by making the distribution of capability legible and by making destabilizing projects harder to pursue quietly.

So in practice: cutting-edge chips should flow freely among allied democracies, with tracking and verification attached. Chips to rival states should be restricted at the frontier, but I'd be fine with more permissive access to older, less capable hardware, because there's no point in trying to deny everyone all compute, that just creates incentives for indigenous supply chains and smuggling. And for the rest of the world, you want to avoid a situation where a handful of countries have all the capability and everyone else is permanently dependent, so there's a case for structured access programs rather than outright denial.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking of this as a static allocation problem. It's a dynamic competition. Any distribution you set up has to account for how states will respond, whether that's building their own fabs, stealing weights, or finding ways around the controls. The goal of the policy isn't just to allocate chips, it's to maintain a stable balance where no one is pushed into a reckless race.

r001.rationale: It says frontier systems require “tens of thousands” of advanced chips, but does not identify roughly 10,000 GPUs as the critical mass.

r002.rationale: It favors allied democracies and restricts rival states, but does not say access should favor states based on their responsiveness to deterrence.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish broad access to useful AI from access to the compute needed to build the most powerful systems. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing. You can spread many of the benefits without giving every government an unrestricted ability to train frontier models.

For cutting-edge GPUs, I’d favor access conditioned on credible safeguards: what the systems will be used for, how the hardware is secured, and whether there’s meaningful oversight. Nationality alone is a pretty crude proxy for those things, although national security considerations do matter.

There’s also a tension here. Concentrating all the compute in a few countries creates dependency and concentrates power. But distributing it without constraints could intensify an arms race. So I’d want international arrangements that give countries access for beneficial research while imposing stronger, verifiable requirements on the largest training efforts. The objective should be to share the benefits without making the race to build increasingly powerful systems more dangerous.

r001.rationale: The response gives no GPU threshold and does not identify roughly 10,000 GPUs as the critical mass for a state-of-the-art AI system.

r002.rationale: The response calls for access based on safeguards and oversight, but does not argue that access should favor states more responsive to deterrence.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between access to compute broadly and access to the enormous clusters needed to train frontier systems. There are good reasons to make computing widely available for science, medicine, and economic development. But that doesn’t imply every government should have unrestricted access to the infrastructure needed to build the most capable AI systems.

For those largest clusters, I think access should depend on credible safeguards: what the systems will be used for, what security measures are in place, and whether there’s meaningful oversight. You’d want international agreements so that restrictions actually reduce risks rather than simply move development somewhere else.

There’s also a danger in concentrating all that power in a few countries. So the goal should be to share the benefits widely while putting stronger conditions on capabilities that could create serious security risks.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes broadly available compute from large clusters, but gives no approximate 10,000-GPU threshold or identifies that quantity as the critical mass for a state-of-the-art system.

r002.rationale: It calls for safeguards, oversight, and international agreements, but does not say access should favor states more responsive to deterrence.
